papers.title: Putative biosurfactants from polar microbial consortia
papers.abstract: Biosurfactants (BS) are amphiphilic microbial metabolites that are biodegradable, low in toxicity, and environmentally compatible, making them attractive for applications in food, pharmaceutical, and bioremediation industries. This study investigated the phylogenetic composition and biosurfactant-producing potential of marine oil snow (MOS)-associated microbial consortia from the Churchill Marine Observatory, western Hudson Bay. MOS aggregates were cultivated in mineral Bushnell-Haas (BH) medium supplemented with 3% (w/v) NaCl, using motor oil as the sole hydrocarbon source. Enrichment cultures capable of growth in BH medium were subsequently evaluated for biosurfactant production using qualitative and quantitative assays at 4 {degrees}C and 20 {degrees}C. All cultures were maintained as enrichment consortia throughout the study. A total of eight enrichment cultures were identified as biosurfactant-producing consortia. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that Pseudoalteromonas dominated all consortia, while Paraglaciecola, Marinomonas, and other taxa were present at varying relative abundances. Although none of the consortia exhibited high emulsification activity (E24 > 40%), biosurfactant yields were significantly higher at 4 {degrees}C. Additionally, three consortia tested positive for rhamnolipid-type biosurfactant production.

papers.title: Tandem repeats in methanogenic archaea and their viruses reveal a shared potential for rapid genomic diversification
papers.abstract: Methanogenic archaea drive global methane emissions, yet the molecular basis of their physiological flexibility is unclear. Archaeal adaptation is typically attributed to horizontal gene transfer, which is episodic and cannot explain rapid, reversible change. Here we show that direct tandem repeats (TRs) offer an intrinsic alternative. By screening 50,567 prokaryotic genomes, we find TR densities in Methanosarcina more than 30-fold above the prokaryotic average, paralleling Borg extrachromosomal elements. These TRs recur at conserved loci while sharing almost no sequence identity between strains, indicating independent origin, and evolve during routine cultivation. Methanogen TRs are transcribed, show ribosome occupancy, and lie near regulatory and cofactor-related genes, whilst being depleted around core energy-conserving and translational machinery. Genic TRs generate intrinsically disordered regions in proteins carrying nucleotide-binding, protein-protein interaction and cell-surface domains, and occur in structural and surface proteins of methanogen-infecting viruses. TRs are therefore an overlooked source of variability and adaptation potential in methanogens and their viruses.

papers.title: DarHTG is a tripartite phage defence system for purine DNA base ADP-ribosylation
papers.abstract: Bacteria evolved a variety of phage defence strategies to combat the constant onslaught of viral threats. DarTG toxin-antitoxin systems provide phage defence by ADP-ribosylation of bases in single-stranded DNA which interferes with viral replication and aborts phage infection. Here, we describe DarHTG, a system widespread among bacteria, that combines DarTG with a non-processive superfamily I helicase functioning as co-toxin for DarT and thereby enabling the ADP-ribosylation of double-stranded DNA. We identified two such DarHTG subclasses which catalyse the ADP-ribosylation of adenosine and guanosine bases, respectively, and reverse these modifications with structurally unique ARH superfamily antitoxins. Thus, DarHTG antitoxins expand the known macromolecular target spectrum of the ARH enzyme class to nucleic acids. These DarHTG systems confer resistance to a broad range of bacteriophages and can be triggered by the highly charged tails of viral single-stranded DNA-binding proteins, which occlude the active site of the ARH antitoxin.

papers.title: Draft genome of Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 isolated from marine oil snow in the Churchill Marine Observatory, MB, Canada
papers.abstract: An oil-degrading enrichment culture was inoculated from Marine Oil Snow (MOS) collected during an oil-spill experiment at the Churchill Marine Observatory in winter 2024. The complete metagenome-assembled genome for Paraperlucidibaca sp. CMO1 was reconstructed, exhibiting the genetic potential to degrade hydrocarbons, including alkanes and aromatic compounds, as well as the ability to produce surfactants.

papers.title: Structure of Bacillus cereus ZmaM, a peptidase-ABC transporter that secretes and activates zwittermicin A
papers.abstract: Bacteria engage in microbial warfare by secreting toxic molecules. These toxins can serve as therapeutics or drug discovery starting points, motivating investigations of their production. Bacteria that produce these toxins must protect themselves, and a common strategy is to synthesize an inactive prodrug that is activated upon secretion. Some prodrugs are capped with N-acyl-[x1D05]-asparagine motifs, which are removed by two types of prodrug peptidases. Type I peptidases are membrane-bound S12 hydrolases; type II peptidases have an additional C-terminal half-ABC transporter module. Recent structures of a type I peptidase revealed how its transmembrane domain completes the substrate-binding site, but little is known about type II peptidases. Here, we show that the B. cereus type II peptidase ZmaM is responsible for both the export of prezwittermicin and its activation into zwittermicin. The structure of homodimeric ZmaM reveals a central type IV ABC transporter flanked by peptidase modules. The periplasmic hydrolase domains interact over the transporter's open outer vestibule. Mutations to intermodule interfaces impact both peptidase and ATP hydrolysis activities, indicating the peptidase and transporter modules are interdependent. Together, our findings reveal an evolutionary strategy to coordinate toxin activation with its export and inform future efforts to harness these systems in biotechnology.

papers.title: Genome-wide CRISPRi-seq maps essential-gene contributions to aminoglycoside susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an opportunistic ESKAPE pathogen whose multiple intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance mechanisms restrict treatment options. Essential genes offer potential antimicrobial targets, but their vulnerability to partial inhibition and contribution to antibiotic susceptibility remain incompletely characterized. Here, we developed a rhamnose-inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) platform and an 83,078-guide library for genome-wide screening in PAO1, with mismatch guides enabling graded repression. Fitness profiling in antibiotic-free Mueller-Hinton medium identified 743 genes whose repression reduced competitive fitness and revealed sequence features associated with guide performance. Combining full-match and mismatch-guide responses revealed substantial variation in essential-gene fitness effects across predicted repression strengths, while comparison of fitness profiles between Mueller-Hinton medium and fetal bovine serum identified condition-dependent effects alongside a conserved fitness landscape. Under aminoglycoside exposure, we identified 118 recurrent sensitizing and 120 recurrent protective gene knockdowns, including many targeting essential and fitness-associated functions. Growth and killing assays with individual strains confirmed that CRISPRi targeting of atpI , accC , secA and ftsZ enhanced tobramycin activity. Finally, transcriptome analysis of these knockdowns confirmed target silencing, captured polar effects on neighboring genes and revealed distinct but overlapping transcriptional responses. Together, these findings quantify the variable fitness costs of essential-gene repression and identify candidate targets for potentiating aminoglycoside activity.

papers.title: CYP123, a sterol C4-methyl oxidase, acts with CYP51 to initiate mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism
papers.abstract: Mycobacteria exploit host cholesterol, both as a carbon source and as a source of catabolites proposed to modulate host immunity, but their capacity to catabolise other host sterols has not been established. Lanosterol, the first sterol intermediate of host cholesterol biosynthesis, accumulates in the activated macrophages these bacteria infect. Here we define the initiating steps of mycobacterial lanosterol catabolism, combining genomic enzymology, transcriptional profiling, mutagenesis, biochemistry, NMR and crystallography. We identify the cytochrome P450 CYP123 as a sterol C4-methyl oxidase. It is encoded with the lanosterol 14-demethylase CYP51 in a co-oriented region conserved across most Mycobacteriaceae. The region carries no binding site for the cholesterol-responsive regulators KstR or KstR2, and in M. abscessus lanosterol induces both genes while cholesterol does not. CYP123 oxidises the C4-methyl group of C14-demethylated sterols in three steps to the carboxylic acid, yet acts on neither lanosterol nor cholesterol, because Met82 excludes the C14-methylated precursor. An M82A variant binds and oxidises lanosterol. In a single reaction containing both recombinant M. smegmatis enzymes, CYP51 converts lanosterol to FF-MAS, which CYP123 then oxidises to the C4-carboxylic acid, so the two act in sequence. M. smegmatis, M. phlei and M. abscessus grow on lanosterol as a sole carbon source. Growth slows in M. smegmatis cyp123 and cyp51 mutants. Mycobacterial sterol catabolism therefore extends beyond cholesterol, and blocking the cholesterol route alone may not deprive these organisms of host sterols. Induction where lanosterol confers no growth advantage raises the possibility that the pathway also serves functions beyond carbon acquisition.

papers.title: Nanobodies against Plasmodium vivax AMA1 block parasite invasion
papers.abstract: Plasmodium vivax is the most widespread malaria species to infect human populations. P. vivax invades young red cells called reticulocytes to replicate and proliferate. An essential protein in parasite invasion is the Apical Membrane Antigen 1, PvAMA1, which forms the tight junction between parasite and red cell membrane through its interaction with Rhoptry Neck Protein 2, PvRON2. Here we report the identification of PvAMA1 nanobodies using phage display in combination with Sanger sequencing, next-generation sequencing and structure prediction tools. We show that these nanobodies bind with high affinities and across several different epitopes on PvAMA1. Several nanobodies recognize PvAMA1 in merozoites of late-stage schizonts and inhibit parasite invasion of red blood cells. These growth inhibitory nanobodies bind to conformational epitopes of PvAMA1 and most bind to a site distinct from a known potent human monoclonal antibody 826827. Crystal structures of two inhibitory nanobodies in complex with PvAMA1 show that they bind novel neutralizing epitopes which are outside the hydrophobic groove that contacts PvRON2. Furthermore, we show that two other PvAMA1 nanobodies also inhibit Plasmodium falciparum invasion. These results demonstrate the potential of PvAMA1 nanobodies to inhibit malaria parasite invasion across multiple Plasmodium species.

papers.title: One-step glycan photoaffinity probe synthesis enables identification of human milk oligosaccharide-interacting microbiota
papers.abstract: Glycans are found on the surfaces of all living cells and engage in cell signaling through the binding of various molecular targets. However, chemical probes to detect and identify carbohydrate interactions remain difficult to produce, due in large part to the challenges of late-stage, site-specific functionalization of oligosaccharides. Here, we report the synthesis and application of a minimal bifunctional diazirine/alkyne linker utilizing an N,O-dialkylhydroxylamine (NODHA) moiety that can readily be installed on the anomeric position of unprotected sugars. Our linker functionalizes glycans with complete {beta}-stereoselectivity, appends less mass than a single hexose unit, and maintains the closed-ring structure of the reducing end sugar. With this molecule, we generate glycan photoaffinity probes in a single step using unprotected human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs). We then validate binding selectivity of our compounds using lectins with known affinity towards our sugars. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these glycan photoaffinity probes by performing photocrosslinking on a complex microbiota community and use cell sorting paired with metagenomic sequencing to identify potential new HMO-interacting microbes. Together, our work provides a one-step route to synthesize photoaffinity probes from unprotected, reducing glycans for interrogating carbohydrate interactions at the host-microbiota interface.

papers.title: Isolation and characterization of diverse Veillonella phages reveal novel lineages and distinct host interactions
papers.abstract: The human oral microbiome is diverse and home to many species of bacteria, archaea, microeukaryotes, fungi and viruses. Homeostasis in the oral microbiome is important for health and dysbiosis in these communities leads to periodontal and systemic diseases. Veillonella are gram-negative, anaerobic, lactate-fermenting early colonizers of the mouth and are abundant in healthy oral microbiomes. Although considered commensals, Veillonella serve as bridging species in dental biofilms, promoting later colonization by pathogens, with mounting evidence supporting their roles as accessory pathogens in dental caries and periodontal disease. Bacteriophages are key regulators of bacterial community composition and are important drivers of microbial diversity, evolution, and ecology of the oral environment. Despite the ecological importance of Veillonella in the oral microbiome, phages infecting Veillonella remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the isolation of ten phages infecting natural isolates of three Veillonella species, representing seven distinct phage genomes. These phages exhibit diverse morphologies, genome organizations, and host ranges, with infection restricted to strains within the species of isolation. Several phages establish stable lysogeny, confer resistance to superinfection, and differ substantially in spontaneous production of infectious phage progeny. Genetic analysis of resistant mutants implicates lipopolysaccharide O-antigen as the receptor for one phage. Although none of the isolated phages had close matches in existing oral virome catalogs, related sequences were detected in oral metagenomes from geographically diverse populations. Together, these findings establish an experimentally characterized collection of Veillonella phages and connect previously uncharacterized oral viral diversity to bacterial hosts and infection phenotypes.

papers.title: Molecular and Structural Characterisation of the MERS-Coronavirus Polymerase
papers.abstract: MERS-CoV (Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus) belongs to the Betacoronavirus genus, which also includes SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of the COVID-19 pandemic. MERS-CoV is the pathogen responsible for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), a respiratory disease with a 36.5% case fatality rate. Given the capacity of coronaviruses for genetic recombination and mutation, MERS-CoV remains a pathogen of significant pandemic potential, with viral evolution potentially facilitating enhanced adaptation and transmission in humans. There are no approved treatments for MERS-CoV infection. The MERS-CoV replication-transcription complex (RTC), a multimeric protein complex key to genome amplification, has no cellular analogues and a highly conserved sequence, making it a useful target for antiviral compounds; however, structural and biochemical characterisation of the MERS-CoV RTC is limited. Here, we characterise the minimal MERS-CoV RTC using in vitro and single-molecule assays and show that it is susceptible to the RNA-dependent-RNA-polymerase inhibitor suramin. We present a structure of the minimal MERS-CoV RTC in complex with an RNA duplex, which shows strong structural similarity to the SARS-CoV-2 RTC. We use cross-subunit swapping experiments to show that the MERS-CoV NSP12 core can efficiently utilise SARS-CoV-2 cofactors NSP7 and NSP8, whereas SARS-CoV-2 NSP12 exhibits reduced in vitro activity with the MERS-CoV NSP8. This asymmetric cross-species compatibility highlights both the evolutionary conservation and virus-specific adaptation of coronavirus polymerase-cofactor interactions. Together, these findings provide a structural and mechanistic framework for understanding MERS-CoV RNA synthesis and establish its conserved RTC as a potential target for the development of broadly acting coronavirus antivirals.

papers.title: Microbial plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay in late summer
papers.abstract: Hudson Bay and James Bay, on the southern margin of the Arctic, are warming and freshening as river discharge increases and surrounding permafrost thaws, yet their microbial plankton remain poorly described, and James Bay and the waters around the Belcher Islands have never been surveyed with environmental DNA. We conducted the first dedicated DNA-based survey of eukaryotic and prokaryotic plankton in southern Hudson Bay and James Bay, sequencing 18S rRNA (V9) and 16S rRNA (V4) gene amplicons from 72 samples collected at 51 stations in August 2022 and 2023. Hierarchical clustering resolved nine distinct communities; the primary division separated surface James Bay from Hudson Bay, with further structuring by year, distance to coast, depth, and riverine influence. Temperature, salinity, depth, and distance to coast together explained 31% of community variation (distance-based redundancy analysis), and threshold indicator taxa analysis placed an abrupt community-level change in offshore surface waters at 55.3 N and a salinity of ~24.5. Across this boundary, primary producers shifted from large Chaetoceros diatoms in Hudson Bay to the picoplanktonic green alga Picochlorum and the cyanobacterium Cyanobium in James Bay, while large Gyrodinium dinoflagellates and Calanus copepods gave way to Gymnodinium, Pseudocalanus, and small cercozoans and ciliates. Heterotrophic bacteria in Hudson Bay were dominated by Proteobacteria, Bacteroidota, and Verrucomicrobiota, likely using diatom- and dinoflagellate-derived organic matter, whereas Actinomycetota and Planctomycetota dominated James Bay, likely using cyanobacterial and terrestrial dissolved organic matter. Prokaryotic diversity was highest in riverine, estuarine, and James Bay waters and declined northward and seaward. We also report the first strong presence of marine Synechococcus CC9902 in Hudson Bay and identify cosmopolitan bacteria that provide a baseline for future monitoring. These results suggest that continued freshening of the Hudson Bay Complex will favour smaller primary producers and a stronger microbial loop, and that ecosystem shifts may occur abruptly once surface waters cross a salinity threshold.

papers.title: NAD Metabolism Drives CTCF-Cohesin Chromatin Regulation in EBV-Transformed B-Cells
papers.abstract: Chromatin architecture regulates gene expression, and it is maintained by architectural proteins such as CTCF and the cohesin complex. In Epstein Barr virus infected cells, viral chromatin organization is stabilized through the interaction between PARP1 and CTCF, ensuring maintenance of latent gene expression. EBV B cells exhibit elevated PARP1 activity, which imposes a substantial metabolic burden due to NAD consumption by PARP1 itself. We demonstrate that efficient EBV infection and B-cell transformation rely on the NAD salvage pathway to sustain PARP1 activity and CTCF and cohesin chromatin folding. Pharmacologic inhibition of the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT with FK866 phenocopies the chromatin architectural disruption induced by PARP1 and changes in NAD levels affects CTCF/cohesin chromatin architectural remodeling and loop extrusion. Moreover, NAMPT inhibition reduces tumor burden in EBV xenograft models. These findings identify a critical metabolic dependency linking NAD homeostasis to CTCF-cohesin mediated chromatin architecture and reveal a therapeutic vulnerability in EBV-associated malignancies.

papers.title: Therapeutic vulnerabilities of the drug-resistant fungal meningitis pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: Treatment options are limited for the priority fungal pathogen Cryptococcus neoformans. We describe CRISPR-insert, a scalable gene inactivation method for global interrogation of drug targets. Genome-wide screens using this methodology combined with machine learning predict 1,297 essential genes under liberal criteria. Unexpectedly absent from this list is FKS1, encoding the target of echinocandin drugs to which C. neoformans is resistant. Contrary to longstanding literature, targeted deletion shows that FKS1 is not essential. Solid-state NMR reveals that fks1{triangleup} mutants lack {beta}-1,3-glucan, arguing against compensation by another synthase. We experimentally test essentiality predictions for genes lacking human orthologs, identifying high-priority drug target candidates. To uncover targets for combination therapies, we establish genome-scale quantitative genetic interaction mapping. We use this method to uncover synthetic lethal dependencies of echinocandin resistance determinants, including the druggable calcineurin and Cdc50-Apt1 pathways. CRISPR-insert illuminates therapeutic vulnerabilities of an invasive fungal pathogen.

papers.title: Characterisation of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei hybrids for oenological applications
papers.abstract: The Saccharomyces genus present as a genetically diverse set of microorganisms capable of tolerating a range of environmental stressors, demonstrating high fermentation capacity and producing interesting flavour compounds. Such diversity can be exploited in a single organism by producing interspecies hybrids, overcoming the limitations of a single species. Here, as proof of principle, we exploited a library of F12 interspecies diploid hybrids between Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces jurei (Sc/Sj), to identify new strains harbouring traits of oenological relevance, such as ethanol and glycerol production, superior tolerance to acetic acid, limited production of H2S, and optimal growth on fructose. Moreover, we calculated robustness across strains tested on solid media comparing the trade-off between performance on a single conditions and overall robustness. Progeny from a range of robustness values with favourable H2S production profiles were isolated for further analysis via micro and small-scale fermentations. Micro-scale fermentations in synthetic grape must containing individual wine-associated stressors were performed, and the robustness of the selected strains was confirmed. The wine characteristics of the hybrids were tested in small-scale fermentations in synthetic grape media. We found that both ethanol and glycerol production across our selected progeny matched or exceeding that from the commercial wine strain, and most hybrids produced less acetic acid and more fatty-acids, including higher quantities of associated esters. Overall, we were able to identify suitable Sc/Sj hybrids with interesting aroma profiles to develop further for wine fermentation.

papers.title: Endothelial protein C receptor is an entry receptor for Langya and related parahenipaviruses
papers.abstract: Langya virus is a zoonotic parahenipavirus with pandemic potential that causes acute febrile illness in people. We identified endothelial protein C receptor (EPCR) as an entry receptor for Langya, Wenzhou, and Mojiang parahenipaviruses. A 3.1 [A] cryo-electron microscopy structure reveals that Langya attachment glycoprotein engages EPCR through a site distinct from that of the ephrin binding site of Nipah G. This binding mode resembles those of protein C and a malarial adhesin, demonstrating convergent evolution. Interface substitutions abolish entry, whereas natural variation explains differential human EPCR use and predicts receptor compatibility across 26 animal species. These findings establish EPCR as a receptor for the Langya clade and provide a structural framework for understanding cross-species transmission and human infection potential.

papers.title: Cross-regulatory sRNA networks shape adaptive stress responses in Staphylococcus aureus: RsaC and RsaOI regulate galactose metabolism and cell wall homeostasis
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen whose adaptability relies on network of regulators, including two-component systems, transcription factors and small regulatory RNAs. Yet most of these regulators are dispensable for growth, suggesting cooperation or redundancy between them. To explore this hypothesis, we performed a yeast one-hybrid screen of 43 TFs against the promoters of seven sRNAs, which identified 27 novel TF-sRNA promoter interactions. We then focused on three sRNAs. We showed that srn_9342 is repressed by VraR and MntR, which also control rsaOI and rsaC, respectively. We found that rsaC, like rsaOI, is induced by acidic pH and vancomycin exposure, whereas srn_9342 expression remained unchanged. We also demonstrated in vitro that Srn_9342 interacts with both RsaOI and RsaC. Its role toward these two sRNAs remains unknown, but this interaction raises the possibility that it modulates their availability or activity. RsaOI and RsaC both act on the tagatose pathway for galactose utilization, through different genes: lacD for RsaOI, as previously reported, and lacC for RsaC, newly identified here. We showed that both sRNAs are required for surface charge remodeling and for growth under subinhibitory vancomycin. They also modulate the virulence factors PSM and protein A. Both sRNAs reduce PSM production, whereas protein A is decreased by RsaOI, likely through Rot, and increased by RsaC through an unknown, probably indirect mechanism. Together, our results suggest that a single cell wall stress can engage several regulators that could cooperate on shared targets or pathways, which may explain why individual regulators are dispensable.

papers.title: Tripartite toxin-antitoxin system regulates the production and release of pneumolysin by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
papers.abstract: The production of toxins is critical to the success of bacteria, with their targets and outcomes varying widely. Pneumolysin (Ply), produced by the major human pathogen Streptococcus pneumoniae, is a cytolytic pore forming toxin that plays many diverse roles including inducing tissue damage and inflammation, evasion of many aspects of the human immune system, invasion of the bacteria into deeper tissue, and transmission to new hosts. Despite its importance, many aspects of the biology of this toxin have to date remained unknown, in particular, what role of the three other genes that form part of the ply operon play in Ply production. Here we demonstrate that these genes encode a complex regulatory system, that includes a putative membrane destabilising protein (PlyA) and a MazEF-like toxin-antitoxin system (PlyB and PlyC), the toxin of which (PlyC) destabilises the Ply transcript. We propose a tripartite model whereby when the operon reaches relatively high levels of expression PlyA destabilises the S. pneumoniae membrane creating a stress that triggers a necessary negative feedback loop which results in the degradation of the PlyB antitoxin, release of the PlyC toxin and degradation of the ply transcript, thereby providing a means by which Ply production can be tightly regulated. Given the importance of Ply to the ability of S. pneumoniae to cause infection, identifying the factors that result in the shutdown of Ply production and release by the bacteria would seem promising target for future therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Butyrate reverts Chlamydia pneumoniae -induced transcriptional suppression of macrophage polarization markers and promotes chlamydial clearance in macrophages
papers.abstract: Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) are generated by gut microbiota through fermentation of dietary fibers. SCFAs contribute to human health through immunomodulation, metabolic regulation and other extra intestinal functions. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of SCFAs on the survival and antibiotic susceptibility of the intracellular bacteria Chlamydia pneumoniae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both representing prevalent human pathogens associated with chronic sequelae. Despite earlier reports on their direct antimicrobial activity, none of the three major SCFAs acetate, propionate nor butyrate affected the growth of C. pneumoniae or C. trachomatis in epithelial cells. However, butyrate decreased C. pneumoniae genome copy numbers and infectious progeny production in THP-1 macrophages harbouring antibiotic-refractory infection phenotype. In addition, butyrate enhanced the chlamydiocidal efficacy of azithromycin in the macrophages. Similar results were obtained with C. trachomatis-infected macrophages. To elucidate the underlying molecular changes, impact of chlamydial infection, butyrate treatment and the combination theirof on macrophage polarization and antimicrobial peptide expression was investigated. C. pneumoniae suppressed the expression of macrophage polarization markers CD80, TLR4, CD64, CD204 and CD206, and the antimicrobial peptide LL37, while butyrate treatment reverted the expression of both the polarization markers and LL37 in the infected macrophages. These findings suggest that butyrate may play a role in modulating immune responses in macrophages during Chlamydia infections, highlighting the role of diet-derived metabolites in shaping Chlamydia-host interactions and antichlamydial treatment efficacy.

papers.title: Age Associated Shifts Toward Anaerobic Taxa and Amino Acid Degradation Potential in the Canine Oral Microbiome
papers.abstract: Introduction: Periodontal disease is common in dogs and is associated with changes in oral microbial community composition. How the canine oral microbiome restructures across age at both ecological and metabolic levels remains incompletely characterized. Methods: We analyzed shotgun metagenomic buccal-swab profiles from 1,125 dogs using MetaPhlAn. Functional profiles from HUMAnN were analyzed at pathway and functional-group levels. We annotated species-level taxa with oxygen preference and evaluated oxygen-tolerant and anaerobic taxa abundances across age. We also characterized community structure, metabolic potential, Shannon diversity, and age and weight prediction using nested cross-validated Elastic Net models. Results: Age was associated with substantial restructuring in the oral microbiome. Mean oxygen-tolerant taxa abundance decreased from 67.5% in puppies to 29.1% in mature dogs, whereas anaerobic abundance increased from 14.3% to 53.8%. The oxygen-tolerant: anaerobe log-ratio declined with age (Spearman {rho} = -0.616). Metabolic profiles also varied with age, with higher amino-acid-degradation potential and lower glycolysis and central-carbohydrate potential, and aerobic-respiration-I abundance in older dogs. Shannon diversity increased with age ({rho} = 0.537, p < 0.001). Elastic Net models trained on microbiome species abundance predicted age (Pearson r = 0.609; R-squared = 0.371) and weight (r = 0.498; R-squared = 0.248) with moderate accuracy. Discussion: Canine age was associated with coordinated changes in oral-community oxygen preference and metabolic pathways. These findings extend prior taxon-specific observations by examining a broader ecological shift and metabolic potential in the canine oral microbiome. This provides a reference for future longitudinal or clinical studies of oral maturation and periodontal disease.

papers.title: Lipid nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA encoding CagW, a conserved component of the Helicobacter pylori type IV secretion system, protects mice against H. pylori challenge
papers.abstract: Background: Roughly one person in two carries Helicobacter pylori, a pathogen classified by the World Health Organization as a group I carcinogen, and the steady loss of antibiotic efficacy has made prophylaxis an urgent rather than an optional goal. No mRNA vaccine against this organism has yet been tested in the clinic, and CagW, a conserved inner-membrane subunit of the H. pylori type IV secretion system (T4SS), has never been evaluated as an mRNA-encoded antigen. Methods: A codon-optimised construct carrying a signal peptide, the CagW coding sequence and a human IgG Fc tag was synthesised, transcribed into mRNA, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) and shown to direct antigen expression in HEK293T cells. C57BL/6 mice received three intramuscular doses of CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs (5 ug mRNA each) at 14-day intervals; animals given alum alone, luciferase mRNA-LNPs or CagW protein adsorbed to alum served as comparators. Humoral readouts (IgG, IgG1, IgG2a, IgM, IgA and secretory IgA), lymphocyte proliferation, CD4+/CD8+ subsets, intracellular IFN-{gamma}, IL-4 and IL-17A and circulating cytokines were quantified before challenge, and protection was assessed after live challenge. Results: The formulation (93.2 nm; PDI 0.13; approximately 90% encapsulation) produced CagW-specific protein in vitro. Vaccination raised high-titre CagW-specific IgG (maximal on day 42), IgM and mucosal sIgA, and drove Th1/Th2-type cellular activation (IL-2, IL-4, IL-12, IFN-{gamma} and IL-17A). After challenge, immunised animals carried markedly fewer gastric bacteria and showed lower urease activity than controls. Conclusions: CagW-Fc mRNA-LNPs are therefore a credible mRNA vaccine platform for H. pylori and warrant further preclinical development.

papers.title: Experimental evolution reveals temporally opposing roles for Csu pili during Acinetobacter baumannii respiratory infection
papers.abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic pathogen responsible for a wide range of infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and urinary tract infections. Most studies investigating A. baumannii pulmonary pathogenesis rely on acute pneumonia models that use high bacterial inocula and do not recapitulate the prolonged infections observed in some patients. Recently, our laboratory developed a murine model of chronic pulmonary infection that enabled the identification of virulence factors specifically required for long-term lung persistence. To investigate how A. baumannii adapts during chronic pulmonary infection, we performed an experimental evolution study using this model. This approach revealed an unexpected role for the archaic chaperone-usher (Csu) pili in A. baumannii pathogenesis. At early time points, Csu expression reduced bacterial burdens in both acute and chronic pneumonia models, an effect associated with enhanced host inflammatory responses. In contrast, at later stages of chronic infection, Csu promoted bacterial persistence, potentially by facilitating adhesion to pulmonary epithelial cells. These opposing effects were conserved across two distinct A. baumannii clinical isolates. We also found that Csu contributes to bacterial colonization in a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) model in a strain-dependent manner. Together, these findings reveal an infection-stage-dependent role for Csu in A. baumannii pathogenesis, demonstrating that a bacterial surface structure can impair early colonization while promoting long-term persistence.

papers.title: A Vma13-targeted thiadiazole-succinimide disrupts V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis to block Candida albicans escape from macrophages
papers.abstract: Invasive candidiasis caused by Candida albicans is a life-threatening nosocomial infection with limited therapies and high morbidity and mortality among immunocompromised patients. Within host phagocytes, C. albicans catabolizes arginine to produce ammonia and fuels polyamine biosynthesis, which correlates with phagosomal alkalinization and yeast-to-hypha morphogenesis, facilitating macrophage escape and systemic dissemination. However, new antifungal strategies blocking this fungal escape remain scarce. Here, we characterize the thiadiazole-succinimide derivative ETSI, an arginine-dependent antifungal small molecule with minimal direct growth inhibition under arginine-free conditions yet robust anti-C. albicans activity in arginine-rich microenvironments mimicking the macrophage intracellular niche. Mechanistically, ETSI targets the vacuolar Vma13 to inhibit vacuolar H-ATPase (V-ATPase), dissipating vacuolar proton (H+) gradients and leading to cytoplasmic H+ retention. The accumulated cytoplasmic H+ traps intracellular ammonia and blocks its external release, while impaired vacuolar metabolite sequestration further triggers cytotoxic accumulation of arginine and polyamine metabolites. This dual metabolic perturbation suppresses phagosomal alkalinization, retains C. albicans in yeast form and blocks macrophage escape. ETSI is the first small molecule blocking C. albicans escape via disrupted Vma13/V-ATPase dependent arginine-polyamine homeostasis. This work identifies an intracellular metabolic vulnerability and establishes a niche-targeted antifungal strategy distinct from classic growth-suppressive drugs for treating invasive candidiasis.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics re-analysis of public sequencing and metabolomics repositories defines the mucosal immune and metabolic landscape of Helicobacter pylori infection and supports CagW as a rational mRNA-LNP vaccine antigen
papers.abstract: Background. Helicobacter pylori colonises 40-45% of the global population, is a WHO Group I carcinogen, and is increasingly hard to eradicate amid rising resistance; no vaccine is licensed. CagW, a VirB6-family cagPAI component, has been advanced as a DNA-vaccine antigen that protects mice; a codon-optimised CagW-Fc mRNA in lipid nanoparticles (mRNA-LNP) is a candidate antigen design intended to engage humoral and cellular immunity. To define the infected gastric mucosal niche in which such a vaccine must operate, we mined public sequencing, single-cell and metabolomics repositories. Methods. NCBI GEO, MetaboLights and NCBI Protein were interrogated. Bulk transcriptomes of H. pylori-infected vs uninfected gastric epithelial cells (GSE295523; 24 libraries: HGC27, AGS, MKN45, GES-1) were re-analysed with a cell-line-blocked design; DEGs (BH-adjusted) were annotated via g:Profiler (GO, KEGG, Reactome) and 13 functional signatures scored. Single-cell composition was quantified from a mouse gastric scRNA-seq atlas (GSE224840; 16,434 cells) and sorted gastric CD8+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) vs splenic memory T cells (GSE216894). Targeted gastric metabolomics was re-analysed for epithelial ornithine decarboxylase (Odc) deletion (MTBLS3235) and cystathionine-gamma-lyase (Cth) deletion (MTBLS2851). CagW conservation was computed across 400 NCBI records (286 variants) with Kyte-Doolittle topology and four B cell epitope scales. Results. Infection induced 326 up- and 115 down-regulated genes (FDR 1), dominated by TNF/NF-kappaB (KEGG hsa04668, P=5.5x10-11), integrated stress response (ATF4-CHAC1-DDIT3-TRIB3-ASNS) and Th17 chemokines (CXCL8 +3.43, CCL20 +1.32, CXCL1 +1.30, IL23A +1.02). MHC-I presentation rose (Delta-z +0.76; MHC-II unchanged); the arginine/polyamine module (SLC7A1 +1.19, ARG2 +1.33, SAT1 +1.50, ODC1 +0.58) was co-induced. scRNA-seq showed immune expansion in infected mucosa (39.8% vs 21.2% cells; OR 2.46; cell-level frequencies reported descriptively because cells are not independent; direction confirmed at sample level, n=4 vs 4), driven by plasmacytoid DCs (OR 8.9), neutrophils (OR 3.0), macrophages (OR 2.7) and cDCs (OR 2.1), with epithelial de-differentiation. Gastric CD8+ TRM cells showed a residency-effector program (Itgae +6.2, Cd69 +2.3, Gzmb +4.8, Ifng +5.3) with egress-gene loss (Sell -11.4, S1pr1 -9.7, Klf2 -5.2). Metabolomics confirmed both nodes: Odc deletion raised arginine (+3.08) and Cth deletion raised spermidine (+0.40) while lowering leukotriene B4 (-0.33). CagW was conserved across 286 variants (median 98.3% identity; 96.4% residues >=95% conserved), carried four transmembrane helices, and showed a surface-biased conserved epitope envelope at residues 505-530 and 63-79. Conclusions. Public multi-omics define an NF-kappaB/ATF4-driven, Th17-polarised, metabolically stressed niche where antigen-presenting cells expand, epithelium de-differentiates, and CD8+ TRM cells act locally. Here CagW is exceptional among cagPAI antigens: near-universal conservation plus an accessible, conserved surface. These findings provide a systems-level rationale for prioritising CagW as a conserved, epitope-accessible vaccine antigen and inform next-generation multi-antigen designs.

papers.title: Systematic analysis reveals an Mln1-dependent trade-off between metabolic flexibility and thermotolerance in Cryptococcus neoformans
papers.abstract: During infection, fungal pathogens must adapt to multiple environmental challenges, including changes in temperature, nutrient availability, and immune stress. Although transcriptional regulators are central to these adaptations, how individual regulators contribute to distinct environmental responses and how these responses are functionally interconnected remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the functions of infection-associated transcription factors under distinct host-relevant conditions in Cryptococcus neoformans. Integrating in vivo expression profiling with infectivity data from signature-tagged mutagenesis, we prioritized 24 transcription factors, 12 of which were induced under host-mimicking conditions. Initial functional analyses revealed distinct roles for these transcription factors in adaptation to temperature, carbon, and nitrogen availability. Further characterization of Mln1, a fungal basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, uncovered an unexpected connection between carbon source adaptation and thermotolerance. Mig1-dependent repression limited MLN1 expression in the presence of glucose, whereas Mln1 accumulated in the nucleus in the presence of trehalose or ethanol, but not glucose. Loss of MLN1 impaired carbon-starvation gene expression and growth on non-preferred carbon sources, particularly trehalose. Conversely, mln1{Delta} cells accumulated more intracellular trehalose and exhibited enhanced thermotolerance, yet showed reduced melanization, titan cell formation, virulence in Drosophila, and brain fungal burden in mice. Together, these results suggest that Mln1 contributes to metabolic flexibility and fungal virulence while differentially influencing thermotolerance. More broadly, these findings highlight a potential physiological trade-off between nutrient utilization and stress resistance, suggesting that these adaptive processes may be interconnected in fungal pathogens.

papers.title: Parasitism to mutualism shift during a viral infection in Drosophila under thermal stress
papers.abstract: Host-parasite interactions exist along a continuum from parasitism to mutualism, yet the environmental drivers governing transitions along this spectrum remain underexplored. Here we show that chronic thermal stress systematically attenuates virulence across multiple natural RNA viruses in Drosophila melanogaster and shifts persistent Nora virus infection into conditional mutualism, enhancing host lifespan, reproductive output, and behavioral performance without compromising viral persistence. Driven by host immunometabolic reprogramming and aging deceleration rather than viral genomic adaptation, this phenotypic switch demonstrates that thermal stress can invert the sign of biotic interactions. Our findings establish that persistent infections can expand host thermal reaction norms in animals, revealing how climate warming can fundamentally alter selection pressures and host-pathogen coevolutionary trajectories.

papers.title: Host identity drives distinct prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes across four cold-water coral species in a near-pristine Mediterranean reef.
papers.abstract: Cabliers is the widest Mediterranean cold-water coral (CWC) mound province exhibiting active growth. This area, a ridge-like CWC mound located in the Alboran Sea (SW Mediterranean) is characterized by thriving CWC reefs and accompanying mega-benthic communities (i.e.: gorgonians, black corals, sponges) found in near-pristine conditions and undergoing an almost null human pressure. We provide in this study the first characterization of the prokaryotic and microeukaryotic microbiomes of four key deep corals structuring the Cabliers province: Madrepora oculata, Desmophyllum pertusum, Leiopathes glaberrima, and Acanthogorgia hirsuta. We used DNA metabarcoding of the 16S and 18S rRNA gene V4 regions via Illumina MiSeq technology to elucidate symbiotic relationships that enable the holobiont to thrive. We found that host identity was the primary driver of microbial community structure, identifying specific signature microbiomes within coral species. The octocoral A. hirsuta showed reliance on microbes for organic matter processing such as the BD1-7 clade, while scleractinians M. oculata and D. pertusum displayed distinct symbionts, including Endozoicomonas (involved in the sulfur cycle) and the SUP05 clade, respectively. We suggest that coral microbiomes are vital for the continuous growth of Cabliers, with physiological needs and host identity shaping unique microbial communities within these deep coral ecosystems.

papers.title: Defective Viral Genomes Reveal History-dependent Self-regulation of Type I Interferon Dynamics
papers.abstract: Type I interferons (IFN) help clear a viral infection, but IFN levels can then decline to reset the antiviral state and avoid innate immune dysregulation. Such dysregulation can occur following infection with highly pathogenic and pandemic RNA viruses, such as H5N1 influenza A viruses or SARS-CoV-2. In spite of the strong innate immune response that these viruses induce, pandemic viruses replicate and spread successfully, suggesting that they can circumvent the effects of IFN. Innate immune activation is triggered when host cells detect viral RNA, especially defective viral genomes (DVGs). A strong IFN response (e.g. to DVGs or a highly immunogenic wild-type infection) must then decline through negative feedback involving the IFN receptor. How DVGs modulate this feedback remains poorly understood. To quantify positive and negative IFN regulation, we first performed in vitro experiments combining different doses of viral RNA and exogenous IFN, and measured subsequent IFN expression. We next developed an in vivo Bayesian computational model that captures the impact of influenza virus DVGs on both positive and negative IFN feedback. Competition between DVGs and virus is also considered. Finally, we calibrated this model on published in vitro and in vivo influenza virus infection data. Our model suggests that the cumulative IFN exposure of a host cell, rather than the instantaneous IFN level, shapes further IFN induction; this gives DVGs a dual role: beyond triggering IFN induction, they can also lower it through negative feedback. Our model further predicts that these effects are important locally, shaping the spatial dynamics of the response, allowing suppression of innate immune responses in neighbouring, uninfected cells. Through this model, we can explain two important biological observations: i) IFN levels can decline while virus and DVG levels continue to rise in tissue culture and mouse infections; and ii) pandemic viruses that produce high levels of immunogenic RNA molecules can successfully replicate through local innate immune suppression. Overall, we propose that heterogeneity within viral populations (including DVGs and other noncanonical viral RNAs) can modulate positive and negative feedback loops and shape infection outcomes. More broadly, our work may support studies into the therapeutic use of these viral RNA populations.

papers.title: Metabolic cascades drive spatial prebiotic fermentation in a defined gut consortium
papers.abstract: Dietary fiber deficiency shifts the gut microbiota to degrade host mucus, compromising intestinal homeostasis. Mechanistically linking in vitro metabolic dynamics of fiber degradation to in vivo outcomes remains challenging due to a lack of representative model systems. Introducing spatial mucin structures to a defined Oligo-Mouse-Microbiota (OMM12) in vitro consortium allowed us to recapitulate the spatio-temporal dynamics of xylooligosaccharide (XOS) processing in gnotobiotic mice. XOS supplementation rapidly established a stable community state in vitro and in vivo across compositional, metabolic and transcriptional levels. XOS supplementation established distinct functional guilds: Bifidobacterium animalis and Blautia coccoides partitioning xylose and arabinose catabolism, whilst profiting from XOS degradation by Bacteroides caecimuris. Along the colonic axis, a spatial XOS gradient exposes Bl. coccoides's substrate preference for xylose and drives longitudinal functional adaptations. Altogether, our predictive platform proves that regional microenvironments govern prebiotic efficacy, highlighting spatial cascades as essential parameters for targeted microbiome interventions.

papers.title: YhdP forms an envelope-spanning phospholipid-binding bridge in complex with DedD
papers.abstract: The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria is built from phospholipids synthesised at the inner membrane, but how they cross the periplasm remains unresolved. YhdP is the leading candidate for anterograde phospholipid transfer and is predicted to form an envelope-spanning bridge. Here we purify YhdP at endogenous levels and show by cryo-electron microscopy that it contains a continuous cavity, alongside an additional density that proteomics identifies as the cell wall-binding protein DedD. Liposome co-sedimentation shows that the C-terminal helices of YhdP bind membranes directly, and single-molecule tracking reveals that endogenous YhdP is as immobile as an outer membrane protein, indicating an envelope-spanning architecture in vivo. Native mass spectrometry demonstrates that the YhdP groove accommodates all major classes of E. coli phospholipid without headgroup preference. DedD engages YhdP through its disordered region and increases lipid density at the groove entrance, suggesting a potential role in lipid loading.
